detailed_rationale:
Cummins India closed FY26 (year to Mar-2026) with consolidated revenue of Rs 11,949.7cr (+17% YoY) and net profit of Rs 2,361.8cr (+18% YoY), domestic sales of Rs 9,961cr (+19%) and exports of Rs 1,989cr (+12%). Q4 FY26 alone did Rs 2,963.2cr revenue (+22% YoY, -1.4% QoQ) and Rs 649.5cr PAT (+23% YoY, +34% QoQ) - but that quarter-on-quarter PAT jump is partly a one-off: Q3 FY26 carried a Rs 126.5cr labour-code-related exceptional charge, of which Rs 32.3cr reversed in Q4, flattering the sequential comparison. FY26 also booked a small one-time gain (Rs 44.15cr standalone / Rs 12.59cr consolidated) from the sale of its subsidiary Cummins Sales & Service Pvt Ltd - immaterial at ~0.5% of annual PAT, but worth stripping out when reading through-cycle margins. By segment, PowerGen (the growth engine) did Rs 4,758cr domestic FY26 (+24% YoY, Q4 +48% YoY), with data centres now 30-35% of domestic PowerGen revenue (35% in Q4). Distribution/aftermarket grew a strong 22% YoY to Rs 3,278cr. But Industrial was flat-to-down at Rs 1,650cr (-1% YoY, hit by extended rains and slow railway/mining tenders), and exports actually fell 6% YoY in Q4 (Europe/APAC only 'modest' growth, Middle East flat) on management's own admission of tariff and geopolitical uncertainty. So two of the four reporting legs are currently soft; all of the growth narrative sits on PowerGen/data-centre.

On the CPCB IV+ angle specifically: the emission-norm transition is not a live pre-buy/post-buy distortion anymore - CPCB IV+ became mandatory for new gensets (19kW-800kW) in July 2023, and the sale of the older CPCB II standard was banned outright from July 2024. FY26's strength is not a rush-to-beat-the-deadline artifact; it is a genuine mix upgrade (higher ASP/higher local-content CPCB IV+ units, especially the QSK60 engine used in colocation data centres) layered on top of a real data-centre capex supercycle. A second, more durable CPCB IV+ tailwind is only now arriving: the first wave of CPCB IV+-compliant gensets sold since 2023-24 begins rolling off standard OEM warranty from June 2026, which should feed high-margin extended-warranty/AMC revenue into the Distribution line (already +21-22% YoY) for several years. That is a genuinely attractive structural annuity. The risk to the thesis is concentration and competitive entry: management itself frames data-centre demand visibility as '3-4 years,' not longer, and Kirloskar Oil Engines has now landed a 192MW data-centre order, pressing into a high-horsepower category where Cummins has historically held an estimated 80%+ share. If that share erodes even modestly while the industrial/export legs stay soft, the growth algebra behind the current multiple gets a lot harder.

Valuation is the crux. Cummins India trades near Rs 5,555/share, market cap ~Rs 1,51,000-1,52,000cr, at a trailing consolidated PE of roughly 62-66x (screener.in shows 62.3x; other trackers ~66x on slightly different EPS bases) and P/B of ~18-21x, against ROE of 30.2% and ROCE of 39.5% - an excellent, debt-free, high-payout (~70%, FY26 total dividend Rs 66/share) business, no argument there. But the 10-year sales/profit CAGR is a much more pedestrian 10%/13%; the eye-catching 23%/31% 5-year CAGR is the current data-centre/CPCB IV+ supercycle, not the underlying trend rate. A 62-66x multiple on a zero-leverage compounder like this is roughly consistent with the market pricing in ~20%+ EPS CAGR sustained for the better part of a decade before fading to a mid-single-digit terminal rate. That is a materially longer and steeper compounding path than management's own 3-4-year data-centre visibility window, and it has to happen while Industrial and Exports - currently a combined ~30% of the revenue base and both soft right now - simply stop being a drag. That is a demanding, low-margin-of-safety ask for a name whose single growth pillar faces rising, well-capitalised competition (Kirloskar, Mahindra Powerol, Caterpillar) and whose end-demand (hyperscaler/colo capex) is itself cyclical and subject to global AI-capex digestion risk.
recommendation_rationale: This is not a business-quality or governance call - balance sheet, returns (ROE 30%, ROCE 39.5%), and dividend discipline are all clean, and the CPCB IV+ warranty-rollover annuity into Distribution is a real, underappreciated-by-headline-numbers structural positive. The call is purely a valuation/margin-of-safety one: at 62-66x trailing earnings the market is pricing a decade of ~20%+ compounding on a business whose own management only commits to 3-4 years of visibility on its single growth pillar (data-centre PowerGen), while the other two-thirds-plus of the franchise (Industrial -1% YoY, Exports -6% YoY in Q4) is currently flat-to-declining. Given the vocabulary here is Sell-or-Hold only, and given how thin the margin of safety is versus a defensible forward growth path, this tips to Sell on valuation stretch rather than Hold, which would understate how far the multiple has run ahead of a realistic 3-5yr growth trajectory.
summary: Cummins India had a genuinely strong FY26 - revenue up 17%, profit up 18%, powered mainly by data-centre-linked power-generation demand and CPCB IV+ emission-norm-compliant products, with the aftermarket/service business also compounding nicely as older engines start coming off warranty. It is a very high-quality, debt-free company with excellent returns on capital. The concern is entirely about price: at roughly 62-66 times trailing earnings, the stock already reflects many years of continued high growth from data centres alone, even though management itself only guides 3-4 years of visibility on that demand and two other parts of the business (industrial equipment and exports) are currently flat to declining. With a well-funded competitor (Kirloskar) now entering the same high-horsepower data-centre segment, we would not add fresh money at this valuation and rate it a Sell on stretched pricing, not on any deterioration in the underlying business.
positive_para: Cummins India is one of the cleanest balance sheets in Indian capital goods - debt-free, ROE 30.2%, ROCE 39.5%, ~70% dividend payout (Rs 66/share FY26). FY26 domestic sales grew 19% and PowerGen domestic sales grew 24% (Q4 +48% YoY), with data centres now 30-35% of domestic PowerGen revenue and management guiding '3-4 years' of continued visibility on that pipeline plus double-digit FY27 domestic revenue growth, backed by India's ~7% GDP growth path and positive infrastructure-budget allocations. The CPCB IV+ transition has also handed Cummins a second, less-discussed tailwind: as the first wave of CPCB IV+-compliant, electronically-controlled engines (sold since 2023-24) rolls off standard OEM warranty from June 2026, the higher-margin Distribution/aftermarket business (already +21-22% YoY) should get a multi-year annuity boost from extended-warranty and specialised maintenance contracts. Cummins also still holds an estimated 80%+ share of the high-horsepower genset category that data centres need, giving it real pricing power and a first-mover manufacturing-localisation edge (QSK60 engine) that a new entrant cannot replicate overnight.
negative_para: The honest bear case is the multiple, not the business. At 62-66x trailing consolidated earnings and 18-21x book, Cummins is priced well above even its own supercharged 5-year CAGR (23% sales/31% profit), let alone its structural 10-year CAGR of 10%/13%. That premium rests almost entirely on one segment - data-centre-linked PowerGen - continuing to compound at a very high rate for far longer than management's own stated 3-4-year visibility window, while the rest of the business is currently soft: Industrial domestic sales fell 1% YoY in FY26 (extended rains, slow railway/mining tenders) and exports actually declined 6% YoY in Q4 with management flagging tariff and geopolitical uncertainty as an ongoing overhang on international demand. Meanwhile the moat in the one segment carrying the whole thesis is not uncontested - Kirloskar Oil Engines has already landed a 192MW data-centre genset order and is investing in the same high-horsepower category where Cummins' ~80% share sits, and Caterpillar and Mahindra Powerol are also present. If hyperscaler/colo capex growth decelerates even modestly (a live global risk as AI-infrastructure capex gets scrutinised), or if competitors chip away 5-10 points of share in the fastest-growing, highest-margin niche, the growth algebra behind a 62-66x multiple breaks down quickly - and there is very little valuation cushion to absorb that.
reverse_dcf_judgment: A 62-66x trailing PE on a debt-free, ~70%-payout compounder is roughly consistent with the market pricing in ~20%+ EPS CAGR sustained for close to a decade before fading to a mid-single-digit terminal growth rate. Cummins' own structural (10-year) CAGR is 10-13%, and even the current supercharged 5-year CAGR (23-31%) is a data-centre/CPCB IV+-upcycle number, not a steady-state one. Management's own guidance - double-digit FY27 domestic growth, '3-4 years' of data-centre visibility - does not stretch anywhere near what the multiple implicitly demands, especially with Industrial (-1% YoY) and Exports (-6% YoY Q4) currently dragging rather than contributing. Verdict: rich. The multiple is pricing near-perfect, multi-year execution in the one segment facing rising competition, with no margin of safety for the two segments that are already underperforming.
